# Deepfake Voice Detection

Deciding whether a speech recording is **real** (a human — *bona fide*) or
**fake** (generated by AI text-to-speech or voice conversion — *spoof*), using
the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access dataset.

B.Tech major project · Team **MP2026CSE309** · Graphic Era Deemed to be University
Supervisor: **Dr. Vidit Kumar**

> **Phase 1 of 8 complete** — `phase-1-complete`. Repository, environment,
> dataset verified, first figure.
> No model has been trained yet, so the results table below is empty.

![Real versus fake, log-mel spectrograms](figures/first_look.png)

A real recording (left) beside an AI-generated one (right), from the training
set. Waveform above, log-mel spectrogram below, both on the same colour scale.
Two things are visible without any model: the real clip has a noise floor
during silence where the fake is nearly black, and the fake's harmonics are
more regular. Regenerate it with `python scripts/inspect.py` — the utterance
pair is frozen in `config.yaml`, so the PNG comes out byte-identical.

---

## What this project is

Not a new model. A careful **comparison**: we fix one simple baseline, then run
six experiments that each change exactly one thing, so we can say precisely
which technique helped and by how much. Reproducibility is the deliverable.

We report **Equal Error Rate (EER)** and **min t-DCF**, never accuracy — the
data is roughly 1:9 real to fake, so a model that answers "fake" every time
scores 90% while being worthless.

---

## Quickstart

Requires Python 3.9+ (we are on 3.12). On Windows use `python`, not `python3`.

```bash
# 1. Clone and enter
git clone <repo-url>
cd deepfake-voice-detection

# 2. Create and activate a virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate     # macOS / Linux

# 3. Install PyTorch FIRST, using the command from the selector at
#    https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/
#    A plain `pip install torch` can give you a CPU-only build.

# 4. Install everything else
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 5. Check the code works before touching the dataset (a few seconds)
pytest -q

# 6. Download the dataset. ~7.1 GB, takes hours, resumes if interrupted.
python scripts/download.py
#    Then delete data/LA.zip to free 7 GB.

# 7. Confirm the dataset is complete and usable. Must exit 0.
python scripts/verify.py

# 8. Produce the first figure
python scripts/inspect.py
```

Step 8 writes `figures/first_look.png`. The utterance pair is frozen in
`config.yaml` (`LA_T_8970804` real, `LA_T_3653342` spoof/A06), so you should
get a byte-identical PNG to the one in the repo. If you set either id back to
`null` the script picks one at random and prints it for you to paste back in.

| What | Command | Needs the dataset |
|---|---|---|
| Run the tests | `pytest -q` | no |
| Get the dataset | `python scripts/download.py` | — |
| Check it is usable | `python scripts/verify.py` | yes |
| Make the first figure | `python scripts/inspect.py` | yes |

## Repository map

```
config.yaml           every setting that affects a result
src/                  all code, one version, always current
  utils.py            config loading, seeds, logging
  protocol.py         read ASVspoof label files
  audio.py            load and prepare waveforms
  features.py         waveform -> log-mel spectrogram
  plots.py            figures
scripts/              things you run from the command line
tests/                pytest, must pass without the dataset present
configs/experiments/  one file per experiment run (phase 4 onward)
docs/                 planning documents and 13 paper notes
phases/phase-N/       what happened in each phase + its artifacts
figures/              committed PNGs
data/ results/ checkpoints/    gitignored
```

**Code lives once, in `src/`.** Phase folders hold documentation and artifacts,
never copies of code. The code as it stood at the end of a phase is preserved
by the git tag `phase-N-complete`.

## The eight phases

| Phase | Weeks | Delivers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–3 | Repo, environment, dataset verified, first spectrogram figure ✅ |
| 2 | 4–5 | All three front-ends, features cached, DataLoader |
| 3 | 6–8 | Baseline model, training, EER + t-DCF, **first reported result** |
| 4 | 9–11 | E1 front-end comparison, E2 augmentation |
| 5 | 12–14 | E3 capacity, E4 duration, E5 loss weighting |
| 6 | 15–16 | E6 fusion, cross-dataset test |
| 7 | 17–18 | Per-attack analysis, DET curves, results tables |
| 8 | 19–20 | Streamlit prototype, documentation, final report |

---

## The six experiments

| No. | What changes | Question |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Front-end: log-mel vs LFCC vs CQCC | Which representation shows fake artefacts best? |
| E2 | Augmentation: SpecAugment, noise, codecs | Does it help on unseen conditions? |
| E3 | Model size: shallow vs deeper CNN vs MFM | Does more capacity help or overfit? |
| E4 | Input length: 2 s vs 4 s vs full | How much audio is needed? |
| E5 | Loss: BCE vs weighted BCE vs focal | How to handle the class imbalance? |
| E6 | Fusing the two best systems | Do they make different mistakes? |

## Dataset

**ASVspoof 2019, Logical Access (LA)** — https://datashare.ed.ac.uk/handle/10283/3336
Licence: Open Data Commons Attribution. 16 kHz mono FLAC. `LA.zip` is 7.12 GB.

We use the official train/dev/eval split exactly as distributed. Attacks
A01–A06 appear in train and dev; A07–A19 appear only in eval, so our headline
number measures generalisation to unseen generators, not memorisation.

| Partition | Real | Fake | Total | Attacks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 2,580 | 22,800 | 25,380 | A01–A06 |
| dev | 2,548 | 22,296 | 24,844 | A01–A06 |
| eval | 7,355 | 63,882 | 71,237 | A07–A19 |
